Analysis: Both hypotheses propose combining IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 inhibition with DNMT inhibitors but differ in target focus. Hypothesis 1 focuses on disrupting a feed‐forward loop that maintains cancer stemness and therapy resistance. It builds on well‐established roles of inflammatory signaling and epigenetic dysregulation, making it relatively more plausible and testable. Although its mechanistic details need refinement and safety concerns regarding combination toxicity must be addressed, its framework is closer to existing experimental validation strategies. In contrast, Hypothesis 2 introduces a novel element by targeting cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and attempting to reprogram them from a pro-tumorigenic to an anti-tumorigenic state. While this concept is innovative, it currently suffers from a lower degree of mechanistic clarity and lacks the robustness in preclinical evidence that Hypothesis 1 enjoys. Additionally, identifying specific epigenetic alterations in CAFs may pose additional experimental challenges, potentially reducing testability and increasing safety risks due to stromal heterogeneity. Overall, given its higher plausibility and clearer path to empirical testing, Hypothesis 1 is superior.
